name: Adenosine (topical hair)

card.summary: A cosmetic hair-growth active with plausible lab data on dermal papilla cells; human evidence not established here.

quick.overview:
Topical adenosine is an ingredient in some hair-growth cosmetics, supported mainly by cell and follicle-culture studies.
A 2024 paper suggests an anti-androgen-receptor effect in addition to growth-factor stimulation.
quick.mechanism: It raises FGF-2 and FGF-7 in dermal papilla cells and prolongs the growth phase; it may also dampen AR signalling. [1][2]
quick.risks: It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient; published safety data are lacking.

lead: Topical adenosine is a naturally occurring nucleoside used as an active ingredient in lotions and shampoos for thinning hair. People apply it to the scalp with the aim of thicker hair shafts, less shedding and denser-looking hair, which improves the appearance of the hairline and crown.[1][2]

In the lab, adenosine acts on dermal papilla cells, the signalling center of the follicle. A 2012 organ-culture study of mouse whisker follicles found that it stimulated dermal papilla growth and lengthened the anagen (growth) phase by raising cysteine levels through fibroblast growth factors 2 and 7.[3] A 2024 paper compared adenosine's gene-expression effects with those of minoxidil and identified the androgen receptor pathway as a candidate target.[2]

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis by Szendzielorz and Spiewak in Biomolecules identified seven clinical trials of topical adenosine, most using a 0.75 percent lotion, in men and women with hair loss, with 466 participants in total. The authors reported that adenosine appears to thicken hair, while describing the trial base as small and often industry-funded [1].

chain: Applied to the scalp as a lotion or shampoo
Acts on dermal papilla cells, raising growth factor signalling
Longer growth phase and thicker shafts
angle.text: People apply adenosine lotions or shampoos to thinning areas hoping for thicker strands and less shedding. Trials have measured hair thickness and density over 3 to 12 months, with a 0.75 percent lotion the most studied form.[1]

infobox: A2B receptor, cAMP, FGF-7 and Wnt signalling in dermal papilla cells; possible androgen receptor pathway effect[1][2]

paras: Adenosine appears in hair-growth lotions and in shampoos combined with caffeine. Reviews of the topical hair-growth market list many cosmeceutical actives marketed through social media, and note that most have been studied as combined formulations with limited sample sizes.[4]

Six of the seven published trials used leave-on scalp lotions, and one used a rinse-off shampoo [1]. Marketed products range from single-active adenosine lotions to multi-ingredient formulas that add compounds such as panthenol, niacinamide, biotin or caffeine [1]. The 2025 review reports that adenosine was absent from 92 hair-loss products sold in Poland in 2018 to 2019, and was present in 3 of 39 trichological shampoos (about 7 percent) sold there in 2022 to 2024, suggesting it remains a minor ingredient among the products on shelves [1]. The review also notes that regulators in the US and EU have approved topical adenosine for skin application at up to 0.1 percent, below the 0.75 percent concentration used in most trials [1].
The review's authors describe topical adenosine products as worth trying, particularly for people in whom approved drugs are contraindicated or cause side effects [1].

In the mouse follicle culture, adenosine increased the expression of FGF-2 and FGF-7 in dermal papilla cells and extended anagen.[3] The 2025 review describes a pathway in which adenosine binds A2B receptors on dermal papilla cells, raising cAMP and FGF-7 expression and activating Wnt/beta-catenin signalling; the authors also note that minoxidil's effects may be partly mediated by adenosine.[1]

The 2024 paper reports that an adenosine complex altered gene expression in dermal papilla cells differently from minoxidil, with inhibition of androgen receptor signalling as a candidate mechanism.[2]

Adenosine is an endogenous nucleoside that acts on adenosine receptors found across tissues. Minoxidil is reported to act partly through adenosine signalling, which gave researchers a reason to study adenosine directly in hair follicles [1]. A broader 2025 review of topical alternatives for hair loss lists adenosine among actives marketed on social media and notes that most have been studied only in combination formulations and small samples [4].

The 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis by Szendzielorz and Spiewak searched PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science from January to June 2025. Out of 8,625 records, seven trials met inclusion criteria, with 466 participants combined and durations of 3 to 12 months [1].

The trials were: a 2008 randomized double-blind placebo-controlled pilot of 0.75 percent adenosine lotion in 30 Japanese women with female pattern hair loss (Oura and colleagues), where the authors reported better hair appearance, growth and loss prevention than placebo; a 2013 randomized comparison of 0.75 percent adenosine with 5 percent minoxidil in 110 men with androgenetic alopecia (Faghihi and colleagues), reported as non-inferior to minoxidil with higher satisfaction in the adenosine group; a 2015 randomized double-blind trial in 102 Japanese men comparing 0.75 percent adenosine with a 0.1 percent niacinamide lotion (Watanabe and colleagues), in which 80 percent of the adenosine group versus 32 percent of the comparator group were rated as markedly improved or better; a 2016 trial in 38 men versus placebo lotion (Iwabuchi and colleagues), reporting higher hair density and proportion of thick hairs and no side effects; a 2018 open-label, uncontrolled 6-month study of 56 men and women with androgenetic alopecia and telogen effluvium using a multi-ingredient lotion (Garre and colleagues); a 2024 randomized single-blind trial of 84 people using a shampoo with 0.2 percent adenosine and 0.4 percent caffeine against a placebo shampoo (Chen and colleagues); and a 2024 randomized double-blind trial of 46 people comparing a lotion of 0.75 percent adenosine, 1 percent panthenol and 2 percent niacinamide with 5 percent minoxidil (Kim and colleagues) [1].

A meta-analysis of three trials of the 0.75 percent lotion at 6 months (Oura 2008, Watanabe 2015, Iwabuchi 2016) pooled hair density (odds ratio 1.03, 95 percent CI 0.89 to 1.20), thick hair counts (OR 1.4, CI 0.82 to 2.38) and thin hair counts (OR 0.93, CI 0.61 to 1.43); none of these reached statistical significance. The authors treated the niacinamide comparator as an inactive control, a judgment that affects the pooled result [1]. Despite this, the authors concluded that topical adenosine appears to increase hair thickness and density and reduce excessive hair loss, while rating the overall strength of evidence as low and calling for larger, better-designed trials [1].

Limitations the review lists include small samples, only three trials with placebo controls, multi-ingredient products that make it hard to isolate adenosine's effect, vague outcome measures, single-center designs, no dose-response studies, and the possibility of publication bias, with four of the trials industry-funded or sponsored [1]. The shampoo trial of caffeine and adenosine was published in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology in 2024 [5], and a broader 2024 systematic review of androgenetic alopecia treatments covers oral, topical and procedural options [6]. A 2024 Int J Mol Sci paper reports adenosine complex effects on gene expression in dermal papilla cells compared with minoxidil [2].

Only one of the seven trials reported adverse events in detail: in the 2013 comparison with minoxidil, 2 adenosine users (3.8 percent; one folliculitis and one itching) versus 4 minoxidil users (9.8 percent, including hair casts and increased shedding) reported effects, a difference that was not statistically significant. The 2016 trial reported none, and the shampoo trial noted dry hair in some users because of the product's degreasing properties [1]. The remaining trials did not address safety [1].

Researchers continue to study adenosine's signalling through dermal papilla cells, including a 2024 report that an adenosine complex altered gene expression differently from minoxidil, with the androgen receptor pathway as a candidate target [2], and the mouse follicle culture work showing FGF-2 and FGF-7 involvement [3]. The 2025 review's authors call for dose-response work and placebo-controlled trials with better outcome measures [1].
